abstract: In the healthy mature artery, vascular cells, including endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells (SMCs), and fibroblasts are organized in different layers, performing specific functions. SMCs located in the media are in a differentiated state and exhibit a contractile phenotype. However, in response to vascular injury within the intima, stimuli from activated endothelial cells and recruited inflammatory cells reach SMCs and induce a series of remodeling events in them, known as phenotypic switching. Indeed, SMCs retain a certain degree of plasticity and are able to transdifferentiate into other cell types that are crucial for both the formation and development of atherosclerotic lesions. Because of their highly cell-specific expression profiles and their widely recognized contribution to physiological and disease-related biological processes, long non-coding RNAs have received increasing attention in atherosclerosis research. Dynamic fluctuations in their expression have been implicated in the regulation of SMC identity. Sophisticated technologies are now available to allow researchers to access single-cell transcriptomes and study long non-coding RNA function with unprecedented precision. Here, we discuss the state of the art of long non-coding RNAs regulation of SMC phenotypic switching, describing the methodologies used to approach this issue and evaluating the therapeutic perspectives of exploiting long non-coding RNAs as targets in atherosclerosis.
body:
Despite extraordinary advances in the understanding of the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis and the use of highly effective treatments, cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide (
https://www.who.int/
). The need for alternatives to cholesterol-targeting treatments has led to an increased focus on investigating other key aspects in the development of atherosclerosis, such as endothelial dysfunction,
1
local inflammation,
2
and the survival of resident and recruited cell types, including monocytes/macrophages and vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs). SMCs are major contributors to the development of atherosclerotic lesions, in part owing to their remarkable plasticity and ability to undergo phenotype switching in response to injury.
3
SMCs dynamically transition into several different phenotypes beyond the 2 classically described as contractile and synthetic, as evidenced by lineage tracing studies and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of atherosclerotic plaques.
4
However, the molecular dynamics underlying SMC phenotypic complexity remain largely unexplored.
Genomic studies conducted in the early 2000s revealed that a mere fraction (≈1%–2%) of transcriptionally active regions in mammalian genomes align with protein-coding genes.
5
,
6
Non-coding RNAs encompass both structural and regulatory RNAs, which typically lack coding potential but, nevertheless, are involved in several essential cellular processes. Regulatory RNAs can be classified by size or by specific structural properties. Short interfering RNAs and microRNAs are small non-coding RNAs, typically 20 to 25 nucleotides in length, that act as endogenous gene silencers. The mechanism of action of small RNAs has been well characterized and used in laboratory research to knock down the expression of desired genes. Sequence complementarity is exploited to target specific mRNAs, which are ultimately degraded within the RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex).
7
Other non-coding species, such as circular RNAs or long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), have broader functional outcomes but are less mechanistically characterized. Circular RNAs display a unique covalently closed loop structure that confers them higher stability compared with canonical linear RNAs, mainly due to the lack of RNAse accessible free 3′OH-.
8
Functionally, they have been shown to be involved in pretranscriptional and posttranscriptional gene regulation by acting on splicing, by working as protein or RNA sponges, and even by generating peptides.
8
A similar functional heterogeneity is to be found among lncRNAs, which represent the largest class of non-coding regulatory transcripts, with ≈127 802 annotated to date (
https://lncipedia.org/
9
). LncRNAs are >200 nucleotides in length and share certain characteristics with mRNAs, including 5′ cap and 3′ polyadenylation sites.
10
Unlike mRNAs, they are not usually translated, although evidence of lncRNA giving rise to micropeptides has been reported.
11
Examples of lncRNAs have been shown contributing to every step of gene expression regulation, from chromatin organization and remodeling to protein translation, acting as gene silencers or enhancers.
10
Their mechanisms of action are diverse and often require structural elements to enable function.
10
A growing number of studies are revealing atherosclerosis-related lncRNAs,
12
,
13
and the improved resolution of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic sequencing technologies, combined with sophisticated artificial intelligence–based analysis methods, are paving the way for a deeper understanding of their contribution to plaque formation by affecting SMC plasticity.
14
Here, we present an overview of the various methodologies used to investigate SMC phenotypic switching in atherosclerosis, with a particular focus on the role of lncRNAs (Table) as molecular regulators of this process in carotid arteries, which is one of the main research focuses of our laboratory, as presented in the 2023 Russell Ross Lecture. We put forward the hypothesis that lncRNAs could serve as potential markers, which could be used, in conjunction with canonical genes, to characterize SMC phenotypes in scRNA-seq experiments and gain insights into the underlying dynamics of plaque formation.
Targeting SMC Phenotypic Switching in Atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis is defined as the formation of a plaque within the lumen of large arteries, including peripheral, coronary, and carotid arteries. A process indistinguishable from true atherosclerosis can also affect vein grafts of long duration, which may result in graft failure.
15
The burden of myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke, which are the main cause of death worldwide, has resulted in coronary and carotid artery atherosclerosis being the subject of the most extensive research.
16
The mechanisms leading to lesion formation are similar across the different systems, although slightly different morphological features can be observed.
17
Atherogenesis is typically delineated in terms of its temporal progression, and, accordingly, atherosclerotic lesions are classified as early and advanced. According to the American Heart Association, the process of plaque buildup can be subdivided into 6 stages, based on histological characteristics, which include (Figure
1
AI) intima thickening; (Figure
1
AII) fatty streaks, with or without macrophages; (Figure
1
AIII) intermediate lesion; (Figure
1
AIV) advanced atheroma; (Figure
1
AV) fibroatheroma; and (Figure
1
AVI) complicated plaques with surface defects, leading to plaque rupture.
18
The latter scenario represents the most unfavorable outcome for a plaque, which, when accompanied by thrombus formation, is likely to cause acute symptoms as a result of impaired blood flow. Advanced plaques may also undergo erosion of the endothelial layer without rupturing. Eroded plaques consist, for a major part, of vascular SMCs and are rich in proteoglycans and hyaluronan.
19
Inflammation is less severe than in ruptured ones and limited to macrophages, T cells, and neutrophils.
20
Thrombus formation may also accompany plaque erosion, although the contribution of platelets is different from the dynamics that can be observed upon rupture.
21
The propensity of lesions to rupture can be predicted by analyzing the structure and thickness of the fibrous cap. This is a protective structure, consisting of layers of SMCs embedded in a collagen and elastin-rich matrix, surrounding a lipid core. A plaque is considered stable if it has a thick fibrous cap (>65 µm in coronary
22
and >200 µm in carotid
23
arteries). In addition to the contractile apparatus, which is more restricted to the cytoplasmic periphery, cap-resident SMCs possess an abundant endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies, consistent with active extracellular matrix production.
18
Plaque rupture occurs when the fibrous cap that covers the necrotic core of the plaque breaks open. With plaque erosion, the fibrous cap stays intact, but endothelial cells (ECs) around the plaque gradually disappear.
Figure 1.
Atherosclerosis in time and space. A
, Different stages of atherosclerotic plaque development are depicted, including the following: (I) intima thickening; (II) fatty streaks (orange), with macrophages (light blue); (III) intermediate lesion, with macrophage and foam cells (light blue); (IV) advanced atheroma with fibrous cap, and lipid-rich necrotic core with infiltrated T cells (green), macrophage and foam cells (light blue); (V) fibroatheroma with fibrous cap and lipid-rich necrotic core with infiltrated T cells (green), macrophage and foam cells (light blue) and apoptotic cells (black); (VII) unstable plaque with surface defects, leading to plaque rupture.
B
, Section of an atherosclerotic plaque showing the localization of different smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypes in region of interest. The corresponding long non-coding RNAs enriched in each SMC phenotype are also listed. Contractile SMCs residing in the media undergo dedifferentiation to mesenchymal-like cells in response to endothelium activation. These cells proliferate and migrate to the site of lesion formation and give rise to fibroblast-like SMCs, producing matrix and contributing to the formation of the fibrous cap; macrophage-like (foam cell–like or inflammatory cell–like SMCs), triggering T-cell infiltration and aggravating inflammation; and osteoblast-like SMCs, secreting calcium deposits, leading to plaque calcification. The latter 2 are to be found within the lipid-rich necrotic core of the plaque.
In the past decade, lineage tracing studies in murine models of atherosclerosis have shown that atherosclerotic lesions are dominated by cells of SMC origin, with reduced expression of canonical SMC markers, such as smooth muscle alpha actin 2 (
ACTA2
), transgelin (
TAGLN
), and myosin heavy chain 11 (
MYH11
)].
24
–
26
The prevailing view is that SMCs in human atherosclerotic plaques also originate from local medial SMCs undergoing phenotypic switch and subsequently invading the intima.
27
Several studies, however, propose that other vascular cells may provide an alternative source of ACTA2+ SMC-like cells, such as adventitial mesenchymal stem cells,
28
pericytes,
29
and fibroblasts
30
or ECs.
31
,
32
Despite being highly specialized, SMCs retain high plasticity, allowing dynamic transitioning to different phenotypes in response to stimuli coming from the surrounding environment, in particular from ECs and inflammatory cells recruited in response to endothelial activation. The influence of the local milieu on SMC function and activities was already known from early studies aimed at understanding the underlying mechanisms of SMC phenotypic switching.
33
After alterations in the equilibrium between growth regulatory and vasoactive factors triggered by EC injury, infiltration of monocytes, and lymphocytes, contractile SMCs residing in the media can undergo transformation in their phenotype that confer them proliferative and migratory capacity. Some of these migrate into the subendothelial space at the shoulder of the growing plaque, proliferate, and initially give rise to fibrous cap SMCs.
34
Each of these founder SMCs retains the plasticity to give rise to other plaque cells with different phenotypes that invade other plaque regions, including the core.
35
Throughout the process of plaque formation, SMC-derived cells are observed to distribute into different regions of atherosclerotic lesions (Figure
1
B). Contractile SMCs are located in the medial layer, whereas SMCs undergoing phenotypic modulation are more abundant near the lumen, at the site of lesion formation.
25
,
26
,
36
,
37
The classification of in vivo described SMC phenotypes is under constant discussion
38
,
39
and a consistent nomenclature is to date still missing. However, it is currently acknowledged that the following phenotypes are involved in plaque development and progression in humans and mice: (1) contractile or canonical SMCs; (2) mesenchymal-like SMCs, in which contractile genes are repressed by KLF4 (Krüppel-like factor 4); (3) fibroblast-like SMCs, which express fibroblast markers (
LUM
,
BGN
,
DCN
,
OPG
) and contribute to plaque stability by synthesizing collagens and fibronectin; (4) macrophage-like SMCs, which might accumulate lipids and participate in the inflammatory state of the plaque by producing proinflammatory cytokines
3
; and (5) osteoblast-like SMCs, which may promote calcification in the plaque and express markers, such as
SOX9
and
COL2A1
. The
KLF4
plays an essential role in SMC phenotypic switching.
24
KLF4 belongs to the KLF family of zinc finger transcription factors and possesses transcriptional repression, transcriptional activation, and DNA-binding domains. KLF4 recognizes GC-rich DNA sequences or CACCC (GT box) and prevents MYOCD (myocardin) and SRF (serum response factor) from binding to the promoter of contractile genes.
40
The stability of atherosclerotic plaques benefits from the presence of matrix-producing SMCs and is threatened by proinflammatory SMC phenotypes. Therefore, modulation of SMC phenotypic switching represents a promising avenue for the development of therapeutic strategies for the treatment of atherosclerosis.
KLF4
has been shown to regulate the transition to multiple SMC phenotypes that are likely to be detrimental to plaque pathogenesis and thus represent a promising therapeutic target.
41
In the following sections, we summarize the recent progress in defining the transcriptional signature of the different SMC phenotypes and discuss further lncRNA-mediated mechanisms driving phenotypic switching.
Toward a Characterization of Intraplaque Cell Phenotypes
As previously stated, lipid-lowering therapies are currently the gold standard for the treatment of patients with cardiovascular disease. The formation of foam cells after the uptake of LDL (low-density lipoprotein) by monocytes and macrophages, and the accumulation of lipids in the arterial intima, represent the initial hallmarks of atherogenesis, triggering inflammation and inducing remodeling processes within the vessel wall. The resulting atherosclerotic lesion harbors a variety of cell types and subpopulations derived from both resident and recruited cells. The characterization of the cellular component of the plaque, in terms of phenotype, markers, and function, represents a significant objective in the process of elucidating the underlying molecular dynamics of lesion formation and development.
Apart from traditional molecular biology and cell culture techniques, the first advances in this field have been made in mouse cell lineage tracing studies.
25
,
26
,
42
Desired cell types are targeted by selecting cell-specific promoters, which drive the expression of inducible CRE (cyclization recombination) recombinase, in combination with different reporter genes. This method allows the migration, proliferation, and differentiation of specific cells to be followed in vivo.
Myh11
is considered the most stringent marker of the SMC lineage, and the Myh11-CreER
T
2 (Cre recombinase-estrogen receptor T2) model has been utilized in many SMC-specific lineage tracing studies.
4
Recently, Worssam et al
43
have generated an SMC lineage–labeled
Myh11
-Confetti murine model characterized by stable SMC-specific expression of GFP (green fluorescent protein), RFP (red fluorescent protein), CFP (cyan fluorescent protein), or YFP (yellow fluorescent protein), which can be randomly induced, allowing clone development to be monitored by scoring monochromatic SMC patches over time. Flow cytometry has also been used to sort cells according to the levels of protein markers of interest. This is not, however, an unbiased approach and limits discovery, as it requires prior knowledge of the sample cell composition. Furthermore, a major drawback for SMCs is the lack of known cell surface markers.
Defining Single-Cell Identity Through Transcriptomics
ScRNA-seq is currently the most powerful technique for providing concurrent information on the cellular composition of plaques and the corresponding gene expression profiles. The field of atherosclerosis research has witnessed a rapid increase in the use of scRNA-seq technology to overcome the major limitations of bulk RNA sequencing, such as the interpretation and deconvolution (ie, the process of identifying and quantifying the relative proportion of each cell type in a bulk experiment) of the transcriptomic signal, as well as the neglected contribution of rare but critical cells whose signal is lost in the noise. In both human and mouse atherosclerosis models, the present cell subpopulations have been meticulously described, contributing to a general understanding of the differences and similarities between the 2 species and, accordingly, the translatability of mouse to human findings.
38
,
44
–
48
Various scRNA-seq platforms and methods are available,
49
including approaches optimized for the preservation of cell viability during RNA extraction.
50
Analysis tools and pipelines, which can even be optimized for the study of desired classes of low-expressed transcripts, that is, lncRNAs, are constantly being released, allowing integrative analysis across single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing,
51
or specialized follow-up experiments such as the identification of rare cell types,
52
cell trajectory analysis,
53
cell-cell communication,
54
and RNA velocity.
55
Of particular note is the latter, which provides an estimate of how mRNA levels evolve within single cells (based on the ratio of unspliced to spliced mRNA over time) and can be used to predict the future state of a cell.
Although scRNA-seq offers a powerful technique, it also presents several significant challenges. For example, the dissociation protocols used for the preparation of single cells from plaques (typically a combination of mechanical dissociation and enzymatic digestion), coupled with multiple filtering and washing steps, can result in the selection of more robust cell phenotypes and the loss of more fragile ones, thus creating a bias in the representation of different cell types in the resulting dataset. The accessibility of SMCs is, in particular, limited by the presence of the extracellular matrix in which they are tightly embedded, by the neighboring adventitia and by possible calcified deposits, which further complicate the dissociation process and may result in the loss of more sensitive SMC subgroups, such as, in our experience, macrophage-like and foam cell SMC subtypes. Furthermore, when removed from their native environment, that is, extracellular matrix, SMCs may undergo phenotypic modification following the absence of the physiological signals and mechanical forces that maintain and affect their phenotype in the vasculature.
56
Other biases may arise from polymerase chain reaction, such as the selective amplification of transcripts with higher expression levels, given that the initial amount of RNA present in a cell is typically low and must undergo multiple rounds of amplification. More generally, each stage of sample processing has the potential to influence gene expression, leading to the emergence of technical artifacts. Spatial resolution of gene expression would be highly desirable, especially within plaques, where cell localization (ie, fibrous cap, necrotic core) is strictly linked to their function.
Coding and Non-coding Signature of SMC Phenotypes
Because genome-wide association studies linked a single-nucleotide polymorphism (rs1333049) in the Chr9p21 locus with cardiovascular risk and demonstrated a strong correlation between this genotype and the expression of the lncRNA
ANRIL
,
57
there has been a growing interest in investigating the contribution of lncRNAs to atherosclerosis and SMC phenotypic switch. Large-scale mapping studies allowed the identification and characterization of many lncRNAs participating in the regulation of SMC transition to different phenotypes (reviewed in Fasolo et al
12
). These usually consist of RNA sequencing applied
58
from in vitro studies,
59
–
62
where defined drug stimuli are applied to polarize SMCs toward desired phenotypes, or human/mouse studies, in which tissue dissected from control/wild-type and atherosclerosis patients/animal models are compared.
63
Besides this effort, analysis of scRNA-seq datasets has significantly impacted our understanding of the non-coding transcriptome of single cells and allowed to gain mechanistic and functional insights on lncRNAs.
64
When compared with level-matched mRNAs, lncRNAs typically display higher cell-to-cell expression variability, as they are transcribed less frequently and with smaller burst sizes.
65
Furthermore, specific lncRNA expression patterns have been detected in transient cellular states, such as cell cycle and proapoptotic states,
65
or have been linked to the development of cardiovascular lineage and cardiovascular disease.
20
,
66
,
67
In this context, it becomes evident that lncRNAs are not only pertinent for the definition, for example, of novel disease biomarkers, but can also be used for the characterization of specific functional cell states or phenotypes.
64
In recent decades, we assisted in an effort in expanding lncRNA databases by exploiting scRNA-seq.
68
–
70
Data integration from different tissues and conditions has facilitated the creation of lncRNA expression catalogs with single-cell resolution.
70
The profiling of lncRNA expression at the cellular level has led to the observation that, similar to mRNAs, a particular (or a set of) lncRNA may serve as a novel potential cell marker.
68
In addition, it has been demonstrated that specific cell groups may exist, which can only be identified by lncRNAs.
69
To date, a considerable number of studies have focused on single-cell non-coding transcriptomes to investigate development and disease.
71
–
73
Although there is a substantial body of literature on single-cell studies aimed at characterizing SMC phenotypes,
45
,
47
,
74
these studies have frequently overlooked the non-coding transcriptome. This represents a valuable yet underutilized resource for investigating SMC plasticity with unparalleled precision.
Here, we present a synthesis of the major SMC phenotypes reported to date in the context of human and mouse atherosclerosis, combining insights from lineage tracing, bulk, and single-cell transcriptomics studies. We highlight the canonical protein-coding markers and explore the possibility of using lncRNAs as a guide to further define SMC phenotypes.
Contractile SMCs
The identity of SMCs residing in the media of healthy arteries has been linked to the expression of several transcription factors, including
MYOCD
,
SRF
, and
KLF4
, which act synergistically to maintain SMCs in a quiescent, contractile state characterized by the expression of contractility genes. Markers of the contractile phenotype include smooth muscle
MYH11
, calponin (
CNN1
),
TAGLN
, and α-smooth muscle actin 2.
75
The cardiac mesoderm enhancer–associated non-coding RNA (CARMN/
Carmn
),
63
,
76
a conserved SMC-enriched lncRNA, is a conserved human and mouse lncRNA that is highly expressed in the aortic media. Its expression is tightly linked to contractile SMC and has been shown to be significantly reduced after 12 weeks of high-fat diet in
Ldlr
−/−
mice, as well as in human atherosclerotic lesions, compared with nonatherosclerotic arteries.
77
In vitro, its knock down inhibits the switch of SMCs to a contractile phenotype and, accordingly, the expression of contractility gene markers.
CARMN
is induced by TGF (transforming growth factor)-β type 1 treatment in a time- and dose-dependent manner via activation of the SMAD2 (mothers against decapapentaplegic homolog 2) and SMAD3 (mothers against decapapentaplegic homolog 3) pathways in human carotid SMCs. Mechanistically, it interacts with transcription factors regulating the SMC contractile gene expression program, such as SRF and MYOCD,
76
and facilitates their binding to the promoters of target genes. In line with these findings, loss of
Carmn
has been shown to be a primary event behind the phenotypic switch to a proatherogenic SMC phenotype and triggers plaque formation in both mice and humans.
63
Interestingly, a role for
CARMN
in maintaining SMC contractility outside the cardiovascular system has been reported in human gastrointestinal SMC,
78
strongly suggesting an association between the expression of a given lncRNA and the conferral of cell-specific properties.
Smooth muscle and EC-enriched migration/differentiation-associated lncRNA (
SENCR
) is expressed in both ECs and SMCs, with different transcript variants associated with different cell types. Interestingly, the SMC-specific isoform is exclusively expressed in contractile cells and its silencing results in the loss of contractility gene signature and subsequent SMC dedifferentiation and induction of a migratory phenotype.
79
Although the mechanism underlying its regulation remains to be elucidated,
SENCR
provides robust evidence for lncRNAs as molecular drivers of cell-specific phenotypes.
The murine myocardin–induced muscle–specific lncRNA (
Mymsl
) is transcribed in a MYOCD-dependent manner in response to stimuli that polarize SMC toward a contractile phenotype in vitro.
80
Mymsl
is SMC-enriched, and its expression decreased in cultured SMC. In contrast with in vitro data, which associated
Mymsl
with the induction of a contractile phenotype, knockout mice showed no substantial difference in the expression of contractile gene signature in SMCs isolated from aortas, whereas, and, almost counterintuitively, a strong upregulation of contractility markers was observed instead in SMCs dissected from ligated carotid arteries. This suggests that different regulatory pathways may be activated by the same lncRNA in different tissues and upon different stimuli. Similar to
Mymsl
, but in humans, the myocardin-induced smooth muscle lncRNA, inducer of differentiation (
MYOSLID
) was found to be upregulated in
MYOCD
-overexpressing coronary artery SMCs, thanks to the presence of CArG [CC(A+T-rich)6GG] elements within its promoter, and provides an example of a contractile SMCs-specific lncRNA marker.
61
MYOSLID
expression was inhibited by proliferation or inflammation-inducing stimuli and promoted upon TGF-β. From a mechanistic point of view, this lncRNA facilitates F-actin assembly and triggers MKL1 (megakaryoblastic leukemia 1) nuclear translocation and the subsequent transcription of SMC contractility gene markers. We propose here
MYOSLID
as a possible complement to canonical protein-coding genes to further contribute to the definition of contractile SMC subpopulations in scRNA-seq experiments.
Mesenchymal-Like and Stem Cell–Like SMCs
As initially discovered in mouse models, plaque SMCs during phenotypic switching tend to lose contractility markers and express to a certain extend mesenchymal or stem cell–like markers, such as stem cell antigen-1 (
Sca-1
),
Nt5e
(encoding CD73 [cluster of differentiation 73]), as well as
Eng
(encoding CD105).
24
,
47
Such states have been described as intermediate stages in the process of SMC transdifferentiation.
39
Mesenchymal-like and stem cell–like SMCs are generally associated with increased proliferative and migratory capacity. Several lncRNAs have been shown to affect proliferation and migration and have subsequently been studied in the context of phenotypic switching.
81
However, many of these have not been strictly associated with a defined SMC phenotype, in part because of the lack of a common reference nomenclature, as its definition is still an ongoing process. Some of these include
NEAT1
, whose expression has been shown to turn off contractile gene markers by acting on
SRF
,
82
MALAT1
, which has been shown to enable PDGF-BB (platelet-derived growth factor BB)–induced proliferation and migration of SMCs by sponging miR-142-3p to regulate autophagy-related 7 (
ATG7
) gene expression,
83
or
SMILR
, which was upregulated in SMC stimulated with IL (interleukin) 1-α and PDGF-BB
60
and regulates cell cycle and late mitotic phase by interacting with CENPF (centromere protein F).
60
KLF4
has been reported as a critical mediator of the transition of SMCs from contractile to mesenchymal-like cells.
24
Interestingly, dynamic fluctuations in the expression of a large and diverse set of lncRNAs as a result of atherosclerosis-inducing events have been shown to correspond to changes in transcriptional programs and SMC phenotypic transition. This was recently demonstrated by Shi et al,
84
who identified the carotid artery disease gene
ZEB2
as a target through which 2 lncRNAs, the
ZEB
-interacting suppressor
(ZIPPOR
) and
TNS1
antisense (2
TNS1-AS2
), exert their function in SMC phenotypic transition. High-throughput knock down studies showed that both lncRNAs regulated carotid artery disease–related cell processes, such as SMC proliferation and migration, in cis (acting on
TNS1
) and in trans. A significant proportion of downregulated genes shared between the 2 lncRNAs was found to be expressed under the control of ZEB2, a master epigenetic regulator of SMC phenotypic transition.
85
In line with this,
Zeb2
selective knockout in SMC resulted in reduced transition SMCs and impaired remodeling processes leading to plaque stability.
TUG1
has been studied in the context of abdominal aortic aneurysm, which is defined as a pathological enlargement of the abdominal aorta due to the loss of contractile SMCs. Induced upon Ang II (angiotensin II) treatment of SMCs and in aneurysmal aortas isolated from Ang II abdominal aortic aneurysm mouse model,
TUG1
transcription is regulated by the Notch pathway. Mechanistically,
TUG1
enables the recruitment of the repressor
KLF4
to
MYOCD
promoter, thus preventing the transcription of SMC contractility markers.
86
Overall,
TUG1
expression in abdominal aortic aneurysm has been associated with dysfunctional SMC and loss of contractility gene signature. It would be interesting to investigate the expression of
TUG1
in carotid SMCs and to explore the effects of its modulation in atherosclerosis murine models.
Macrophage-Like SMCs
Recent studies now recognize that a substantial proportion of foam cells found in human and murine atherosclerotic plaques, characterized by the accumulation of intracellular lipid droplets as a consequence of cholesterol overload and downregulation of ABCA1 (ATP-binding cassette transporter-1), are derived from SMCs rather than myeloid cells.
87
,
88
By using a lineage tracing approach, Feil et al
25
showed that SMCs can differentiate into a macrophage-like phenotype in vivo. Bashore et al
89
confirmed the presence of an
ACTA2+
macrophage subpopulation that also expressed sustained levels of other SMC-related genes, such as
MYOCD
,
MYH11
, and
CNN1
, in human atherosclerotic plaques. In the literature, the term macrophage-like SMC has been used to refer to SMCs expressing macrophage-associated genes, foam cells, and cells with a transcriptional profile overlapping that of bone marrow–derived macrophages, although the SMC origin of the latter has been questioned. Macrophage-like SMCs expressed the macrophage markers
CD68
and galectin-3 (
LGALS3
). Interestingly,
LGALS3
expression has been detected not only in cholesterol-loaded in vitro populations of SMCs
90
but also in SMCs entering transitional state, possessing stem cell–like features and capable of extracellular matrix remodeling, although not exhibiting foam cell features.
41
Compared with macrophages, macrophage-like SMCs have overall low level of lysosomal acid lipase, so their ability to catabolize lipoproteins is lower, and therefore, they are more likely to become foam cells.
87
,
88
It is, however, still under debate whether SMCs acquire a macrophage-like phenotype and then become foam cells or whether they express macrophage markers after becoming foam cells. The high level of dynamicity underlying phenotypic switching makes the classification of SMC phenotypes a challenging task. We think that lncRNA expression profiling could be a valuable tool to more accurately describe the different shades of SMC phenotypes. Our group has shown that the lncRNA myocardial infarction-associated transcript (
MIAT
) promotes the phenotypic transition of SMCs to proinflammatory, macrophage-like cells by regulating
KLF4
expression and further induces proliferation and migration by acting on the EGR1 (early growth response 1)-ELK1 (ETS-like transcription factor 1)-ERK (extracellular signal–regulated kinase) pathway.
91
The above-mentioned lncRNA
ANRIL
has been shown to be upregulated in patients with coronary atherosclerotic heart disease and in ox-LDL (oxidized LDL)–induced phenotypic transition of human aortic SMC to foam cells.
92
Zhang et al
92
described a previously unidentified mechanism of action whereby
ANRIL
increases the expression of reactive oxygen species–related genes, such as
NOX1
. The lncRNA may act as a molecular scaffold that facilitates the formation of chromatin-modifying complexes (WDR5 [WD repeat domain 5] and HDAC3 [histone deacetylase 3]) regulating the expression of target genes. This provides a novel epigenetic regulatory mechanism responsible for the phenotypic transition of SMC, which can be modulated by targeting
ANRIL
. In another work, a lncRNA named
HSPA7
has been shown to promote the transition to an inflammatory cell type in human atherosclerotic plaques. When induced by ox-LDL, it sponges miR-223, leading to the expression of the NOD-, LRR-, and pyrin domain–containing protein 3 (
NLRP3
) inflammasome.
93
The inflammatory
MKL1
-interacting lncRNA (
INKILN
) is downregulated in contractile SMCs and upregulated in human atherosclerosis. Induced upon vascular injury, it activates SMC inflammatory pathways in synergy with
MKL1
and exacerbates neointimal formation, as demonstrated in vitro and ex vivo in culture vessels.
94
In particular, injured carotids of transgenic mice expressing the human
INKILN
displayed increased inflammatory cell infiltration and cell proliferation, compared with wild-type controls. It would be interesting to investigate whether the transition to macrophage-like states occurs via an intermediate step (ie, mesenchymal) or whether it exclusively involves a direct switch from contractile to macrophage-like SMC and to more accurately profile the expression of
MIAT
,
ANRIL
,
HSPA7
, and
INKILN
during the transition, to investigate whether these are activating the transition process itself or if they instead contribute to polarizing cells toward a specific phenotype.
Fibroblast-Like SMCs
As introduced earlier, the transition of SMCs to synthetic fibrotic SMCs is thought to be beneficial for plaque stability, as these cells build the fibrous cap. Several scRNA-seq studies focused on human atherosclerosis have indicated the presence of SMCs with intermediate characteristics between fibroblasts and canonical SMCs. Hao et al
95
called them myofibroblast-like, characterized by reduced or no expression of
MYH11
and
SMTN
, but no specific markers to distinguish them from SMCs. Transdifferentiation of SMCs to such a phenotype is a disease-related process, as myofibroblasts are usually rarely found in healthy vessels.
95
Other studies have described the presence of fibroblast-like SMCs (or fibromyocytes) in human and mouse atherosclerotic lesions, with upregulated expression of fibroblast-related genes. In addition to
ACTA2
and other contractility markers, fibroblast-like SMCs express mesenchymal genes, although subsequent studies show that these represent 2 distinct cell types.
47
A clear line of demarcation between fibroblast-like, myofibroblast-like, and canonical SMCs is yet to be defined, primarily because of the dynamic nature of phenotypic switching itself. We think that lncRNAs may come to the aid of currently available protein-coding markers to address the aforementioned gap. Ongoing studies supporting this view have (1) provided evidence of key lncRNA regulators of the fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition in fibrosis
94
and, more in general, (2) reported that specific cell groups may exist, as revealed by scRNA-seq, that can only be identified by utilizing lncRNAs.
69

Osteoblast-Like SMCs
Vascular calcification consists of the deposition of hydroxyapatite crystals in the intima and media. It is prevalent in advanced atherosclerotic lesions and results from the transition of contractile SMCs to an osteoblast-like phenotype, characterized by the formation of calcified vesicles and the production of a calcification-prone matrix.
97
Calcification markers include RUNX2 (Runt-related transcription factor 2), SRY-box transcription factor 9, osteopontin, osteocalcin, alkaline phosphatase, osterix, and collagen types II and X. Expression of the lncRNAs
GAS5
98
and
Lrrc75a-as1
99
was inversely correlated with calcified human and rat SMCs, respectively.
MALAT1
has recently been proposed to promote the calcification of human SMCs via miR-30c sponging and regulation of Runx2 expression.
100
LncRNA-ES3
regulates high glucose–induced calcification/senescence of SMCs via the miR-34c-5p/BMF (Bcl2 modifying factor) axis.

Advent of Spatial Transcriptomics
The atherosclerotic plaque provides an illustrative example of how tissue context facilitates the assessment of cell biology. In the study of SMC phenotypic switching, the mapping of the localization of identified cell clusters would also assist in associating them with specific functional characteristics, which, in turn, may contribute to a more accurate prognosis of lesion development. Advances in mass spectrometry imaging and improvements in its resolution have enabled spatially resolved, high-throughput molecular analysis of proteins, peptides, metabolites, lipids, and drugs directly in tissue.
102
,
103
Although proteomics approaches, like deep visual proteomics,
102
are extremely useful for revealing molecular features of complex tissues as mRNA abundance and location do not always mirror the ones of proteins, they do not cover the non-coding transcriptome, which, as discussed in the lecture, represents the majority of the transcriptional output of cells and can be of great help in characterizing single cells populating tissues. The development of high-throughput techniques for transcript visualization has become important in this field.

An increasing number of commercially available platforms are now available for high-throughput in situ assessment of gene transcription, including whole-transcriptome-targeted spatial transcriptomics,
104

GeoMx

from Nanostring. These take advantage of barcoded oligonucleotides for transcript capture and overall are limited to a spatial resolution of up to 55 to 100 µm owing to the physical size of capturing spots. Both technologies have been improved to reach subcellular resolution with
Visium-HD

platforms. Although

CosMx
platform currently stands with a limited transcript coverage (6000-plex). A major drawback coming along with increased spatial resolution is, however, the decreased detectability of lowly abundant transcripts, due to the limits of sequencing depths that can be reached. Similar to
CosMx

109
A caveat, in this context, is that most commercially available gene panels do not include lncRNAs or, alternatively, include the ones displaying higher expression levels, thus requiring user-defined custom probes. Spatial transcriptomics represents a valid complement to scRNA-seq analysis, particularly when the objective is to obtain viable cells from whole tissue without inducing stress, cell death, and cell aggregation. In fact, in contrast to immune cells, which are not always firmly anchored in the tissue and are, therefore, more accessible for scRNA-seq studies, as previously mentioned, SMCs in the vasculature require specific dissociation procedures, which introduce technical biases that may affect the quality of the results. Although numerous platforms currently allow to resolve spatial gene expression at subcellular resolution, a crucial challenge is represented by the employment of different cell segmentation criteria adopted to allocate signals to individual cells. For example, the first release of 10× Genomics
Xenium
utilized DAPI (4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) to identify the nucleus and expanded the perimeter to detect the optimal limits defining each cell. In contrast, CosMx employs both DAPI and membrane staining to identify both cell compartments. Such discrepancies may present obstacles to a comprehensive comparison of the various platforms. The combination of scRNA-seq data and spatial transcriptomics represents a promising approach to understand cellular heterogeneity in its spatial context.
110
Currently, many computational tools are being developed to map individual cells from a scRNA-seq dataset to spatial expression profiles, such as STEM
111
and cytoSPACE.
112
Furthermore, Cell2location
113
provides a probabilistic model for the precise assignment of cell types in tissue samples, and SpatialDWLS
114
represents instead a powerful deconvolution methodology to disentangle spatial data based on single-cell references. Altogether, the selection of an appropriate spatial transcriptomic method is crucial and highly dependent on the desired spatial resolution, the tissue area, the sensitivity of RNA detection, and the number of genes to be profiled. In the context of SMC plasticity in atherosclerosis, targeted spatial transcriptomics approaches using preselected markers for in situ profiling could be suitable approaches to capture macrophage-like and foam cell–like SMC subtypes, which are either underrepresented or completely lost during the extraction procedures and library preparation steps of current single-cell sequencing technologies.
As previously discussed, technological advancements have enabled researchers to approach issues related to atherosclerosis and SMC phenotypic switching from multiple perspectives, providing alternative yet often complementary information. The ability to integrate knowledge derived from diverse sources, including not only -omics datasets but also clinical practice, animal models, and laboratory experiments, represents a powerful tool for a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular and cellular dynamics underlying disease (Figure

A holistic approach to investigate smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic switching in atherosclerosis.
A multidisciplinary approach can be adopted to investigate the complexity of phenotypic switching in atherosclerosis. Knowledge acquired from patient-related clinical information, histopathologic hallmarks of plaques, animal models, and omics datasets can be combined for a better understanding of the molecular and cellular dynamics underlying disease. Data integration can be performed at different levels. Some examples include (1) in bulk RNA sequencing experiments, where the contribution of single cells to disease-linked dynamics of differential gene expression cannot be assessed, the quantification of the relative proportion of each cell type in the starting sample can be computationally inferred by utilizing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data as reference gene expression profiles from known cell types or subpopulations (a process known as deconvolution); (2) scRNA-seq can complement lineage tracing studies in defining markers (both non-coding and protein coding) of SMC subpopulations; (3) the combination of scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics allows to investigate cell-cell interactions; (4) machine learning (ML) techniques can be used to integrate histopathologic data with spatial -omics data. GWAS indicates genome-wide association studies.
Concluding Remarks and Outlook
The capacity of SMCs to adopt diverse phenotypes is a pivotal factor in vascular remodeling and the formation of atherosclerotic plaques. For this reason, SMCs have been the subject of particular scrutiny in scRNA-seq studies. These techniques enabled the analysis of single-cell transcriptomes with unprecedented precision, facilitating the acquisition of novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underpinning SMC plasticity. Accessing the non-coding transcriptome of single cells and investigating non-coding species represents a crucial resource for a more comprehensive characterization of the diverse SMC phenotypes. Given their highly cell-specific expression profiles and their well-documented involvement in developmental, physiological, and disease-related biological processes, lncRNAs represent a promising avenue for further investigation into yet-to-be-explored hot topics, such as clonal expansion, in the pursuit of the molecular drivers of SMC phenotypic switching. In a more long-term therapeutic perspective of targeting SMC phenotypic switching to reduce the burden of atherosclerosis, lncRNAs may offer untapped druggable targets that might complement protein-coding genes. Current clinical trials on lncRNAs are for now focused on lncRNA biomarker potential, mainly in cancer (
https://clinicaltrials.gov/search?term=Long%20Noncoding%20RNA
). It seems to be only a matter of time before the first therapeutic intervention studies targeting lncRNAs (using antisense oligonucleatides or short interfering RNAs) will emerge.
